claim: Type I interferon (IFN-I) responses are critical for the control of RNA virus infections.
source: Type I interferon (IFN-I) responses are critical for the control of RNA virus infections, however, many viruses, including Dengue (DENV) and Chikungunya (CHIKV) virus, do not directly activate plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), robust IFN-I producing cells.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of virology and immunology.

claim: Many viruses, including Dengue (DENV) and Chikungunya (CHIKV) virus, do not directly activate plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs).
source: Type I interferon (IFN-I) responses are critical for the control of RNA virus infections, however, many viruses, including Dengue (DENV) and Chikungunya (CHIKV) virus, do not directly activate plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), robust IFN-I producing cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's own experimental findings and citations to prior work.

claim: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) are robust IFN-I producing cells.
source: Type I interferon (IFN-I) responses are critical for the control of RNA virus infections, however, many viruses, including Dengue (DENV) and Chikungunya (CHIKV) virus, do not directly activate plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), robust IFN-I producing cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about pDC function.

claim: DENV and CHIKV infected cells are sensed by pDCs indirectly.
source: Herein, we demonstrated that DENV and CHIKV infected cells are sensed by pDCs, indirectly, resulting in selective IRF7 activation and IFN-I production, in the absence of other inflammatory cytokine responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Indirect sensing of DENV and CHIKV infected cells by pDCs results in selective IRF7 activation and IFN-I production.
source: Herein, we demonstrated that DENV and CHIKV infected cells are sensed by pDCs, indirectly, resulting in selective IRF7 activation and IFN-I production, in the absence of other inflammatory cytokine responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including cytokine measurements and gene expression analysis.

claim: Indirect sensing of DENV and CHIKV infected cells by pDCs occurs in the absence of other inflammatory cytokine responses.
source: Herein, we demonstrated that DENV and CHIKV infected cells are sensed by pDCs, indirectly, resulting in selective IRF7 activation and IFN-I production, in the absence of other inflammatory cytokine responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing lack of TNFα and other NF-κB-dependent cytokines.

claim: A mouse model was developed in which IRF7 signaling is restricted to pDCs.
source: To elucidate pDC immunomodulatory functions, we developed a mouse model in which IRF7 signaling is restricted to pDC.
evidence: This is supported by the description of the SiglechIrf7/+;Irf3-/-;Irf7-/- mouse model generation.

claim: pDC-restricted IRF7 signaling controlled both DENV and CHIKV viruses despite undetectable levels of IFN-I protein.
source: Despite undetectable levels of IFN-I protein, pDC-restricted IRF7 signaling controlled both viruses and was sufficient to protect mice from lethal CHIKV infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data and IFN-I measurements in the pDC:Irf7+ mouse model.

claim: pDC-restricted IRF7 signaling was sufficient to protect mice from lethal CHIKV infection.
source: Despite undetectable levels of IFN-I protein, pDC-restricted IRF7 signaling controlled both viruses and was sufficient to protect mice from lethal CHIKV infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data showing 100% survival in pDC:Irf7+ mice compared to lethal infection in Irf3/7 DKO mice.

claim: Early pDC IRF7-signaling resulted in amplification of downstream antiviral responses, including an accelerated natural killer (NK) cell-mediated type II IFN response.
source: Early pDC IRF7-signaling resulted in amplification of downstream antiviral responses, including an accelerated natural killer (NK) cell-mediated type II IFN response.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing earlier IFNγ production by NK cells in pDC:Irf7+ mice compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice.

claim: pDC IRF7-signaling plays a dominant, yet indirect role in directing both type I and II IFN responses during arbovirus infections.
source: These studies revealed the dominant, yet indirect role of pDC IRF7-signaling in directing both type I and II IFN responses during arbovirus infections.
evidence: This claim is supported by the overall experimental findings showing pDC-mediated control of both IFN-I and IFN-II responses.

claim: Viral sensing may involve non-hematopoietic or hematopoietic cells that are targets of infection.
source: Viral sensing may involve non-hematopoietic or hematopoietic cells that are targets of infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of viral immunology.

claim: Specific pathogen-associated motifs, such as viral nucleic acids, are recognized by pattern recognition receptors.
source: Specific pathogen-associated motifs, such as viral nucleic acids, are recognized by pattern recognition receptors, which can be cytoplasmic (e.g. retinoic inducible gene-I (RIG-I)-like receptors, and NOD-like Receptors) or endosomal (e.g. Toll-like receptors; TLRs) (Jensen and Thomsen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jensen and Thomsen, 2012.

claim: Pattern recognition receptors can be cytoplasmic (e.g. RIG-I-like receptors, and NOD-like Receptors) or endosomal (e.g. Toll-like receptors; TLRs).
source: Specific pathogen-associated motifs, such as viral nucleic acids, are recognized by pattern recognition receptors, which can be cytoplasmic (e.g. retinoic inducible gene-I (RIG-I)-like receptors, and NOD-like Receptors) or endosomal (e.g. Toll-like receptors; TLRs) (Jensen and Thomsen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jensen and Thomsen, 2012.

claim: Most viruses have evolved mechanisms to subvert or evade pathogen-sensing pathways.
source: Due to the potency of these innate responses, most viruses have evolved mechanisms to subvert or evade pathogen-sensing pathways (GarciaGarcía-Sastre, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to García-Sastre, 2017.

claim: Alternative or indirect pathogen-sensing mechanisms exist that circumvent cell-intrinsic viral evasion mechanisms.
source: We and others have recently highlighted the existence of alternative or indirect pathogen-sensing mechanisms that circumvents cell-intrinsic viral evasion mechanisms (Webster et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Webster et al., 2016.

claim: Alternative pathogen-sensing pathways involve the sensing of infected target cells by plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs).
source: Such alternative pathways involve the sensing of infected target cells by plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), a DC subtype specialized in the production of robust level of type I IFNs (referred herein to as IFN-I) (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Swiecki and Colonna, 2015.

claim: pDCs are a DC subtype specialized in the production of robust level of type I IFNs.
source: Such alternative pathways involve the sensing of infected target cells by plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), a DC subtype specialized in the production of robust level of type I IFNs (referred herein to as IFN-I) (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Swiecki and Colonna, 2015.

claim: Dengue virus (DENV) is a positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus that represents global health concerns.
source: Notably, this was illustrated in the context of dengue virus (DENV), a positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus, which represents global health concerns (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bhatt et al., 2013.

claim: A newly defined mode of pDC activation is mediated primarily by non-infectious immature DENV particles and requires physical cell-cell contact with DENV-infected cells.
source: Recent in vitro work highlighted a newly defined mode of pDC activation, which is mediated primarily by non-infectious immature DENV particles and requires physical cell-cell contact with DENV-infected cells (Décembre et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Décembre et al., 2014.

claim: Cell-cell contact-dependent activation of pDCs has been reported for several other genetically distant viruses.
source: Importantly, such cell-cell contact-dependent activation of pDCs has also been reported for several other genetically distant viruses (Webster et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Webster et al., 2016.

claim: DENV does not directly infect pDCs.
source: Consistently, DENV, like some other viruses, does not to directly infect pDCs (Décembre et al., 2014; Webster et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Décembre et al., 2014 and Webster et al., 2016.

claim: pDCs function as sentinels of viral infection, predominantly via recognition of single-stranded RNA and unmethylated CpG containing DNA by endosomal TLR7 and TLR9, respectively.
source: pDCs function as sentinels of viral infection, predominantly via recognition of single-stranded RNA and unmethylated CpG containing DNA by endosomal TLR7 and TLR9, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pDC function.

claim: Activation of TLR7 or TLR9 results in copious secretion of IFN-I as well as other proinflammatory cytokines (notably TNFα), driven by the transcription factor(s) interferon regulatory factor (IRF)−7 and nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB), respectively.
source: Activation of TLR7 or TLR9 results in copious secretion of IFN-I as well as other proinflammatory cytokines (notably TNFα), driven by the transcription factor(s) interferon regulatory factor (IRF)−7 and nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB), respectively (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Swiecki and Colonna, 2015.

claim: Previous studies have suggested a 'bifurcated' pattern of TLR7/9 signaling, where IFN-I production may occur in the absence of NF-κB activation, and vice versa.
source: Interestingly, despite the inherent ability of pDCs to produce both IFN-I and NF-κB-induced cytokines, previous studies have suggested a 'bifurcated' pattern of TLR7/9 signaling, where IFN-I production may occur in the absence of NF-κB activation, and vice versa (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Swiecki and Colonna, 2015.

claim: The production of IFN-I or pro-inflammatory cytokines may in part be dependent on the sub-cellular compartment in which TLRs encounter activating signal.
source: The production of IFN-I or pro-inflammatory cytokines may in part be dependent on the sub-cellular compartment in which these TLRs encounter activating signal, as CpG-A accumulates in early endosomes to induce IFN-I whereas CpG-B aggregates in endolysosomes to activate NF-κB (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Swiecki and Colonna, 2015.

claim: CpG-A accumulates in early endosomes to induce IFN-I whereas CpG-B aggregates in endolysosomes to activate NF-κB.
source: The production of IFN-I or pro-inflammatory cytokines may in part be dependent on the sub-cellular compartment in which these TLRs encounter activating signal, as CpG-A accumulates in early endosomes to induce IFN-I whereas CpG-B aggregates in endolysosomes to activate NF-κB (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Swiecki and Colonna, 2015.

claim: pDCs exposed to cell-associated Hepatitis C virus produced IFN-I but not NF-κB-dependent cytokines.
source: In the context of viral infection, pDCs exposed to cell-associated Hepatitis C virus produced IFN-I but not NF-κB-dependent cytokines (Dental et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dental et al., 2012.

claim: The sensing of DENV-infected cells by human pDCs failed to induce TNFα secretion.
source: The sensing of DENV-infected cells by human pDCs failed to induce TNFα secretion (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Direct TLR7 stimuli, including the synthetic ligand imiquimod (IMQ) and influenza A [Flu], trigger robust TNFα production by pDCs.
source: This was in contrast to the robust TNFα production triggered by direct TLR7 stimuli, including the synthetic ligand imiquimod (IMQ) and influenza A [Flu], which directly activates pDCs as cell-free virus as previously reported (Décembre et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and citation to Décembre et al., 2014.

claim: Influenza A directly activates pDCs as cell-free virus.
source: This was in contrast to the robust TNFα production triggered by direct TLR7 stimuli, including the synthetic ligand imiquimod (IMQ) and influenza A [Flu], which directly activates pDCs as cell-free virus as previously reported (Décembre et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Décembre et al., 2014.

claim: IFNβ pretreatment has been previously shown to accelerate both IFNα and TNFα production in response to influenza virus.
source: Such pre-treatment regimens have been previously shown to accelerate both IFNα and TNFα production in response to influenza virus (Phipps-Yonas et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Phipps-Yonas et al., 2008.

claim: IFNβ pretreatment accelerated the kinetics of pDC-derived IFNα (all stimuli) and TNFα production (IMQ/Flu), but minimal TNFα production was observed in response to DENV-infected cells.
source: While IFNβ pretreatment accelerated the kinetics of pDC-derived IFNα (all stimuli) and TNFα production (IMQ/Flu), we observed minimal TNFα production in response to DENV-infected cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The defect in DENV-mediated TNFα induction by pDCs might be due to the indirect mechanism of stimulation.
source: These observations imply that the defect in DENV-mediated TNFα induction by pDCs might be due to the indirect mechanism of stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: pDC TNFα levels in response to IMQ were not diminished in presence of DENV-infected cells.
source: Furthermore, we showed that pDC TNFα levels in response to IMQ were not diminished in presence of DENV-infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DENV is neither promoting nor preventing the activation of NF-κB-induced TNFα production by pDCs.
source: Together, these results indicated that DENV is neither promoting nor preventing the activation of NF-κB-induced TNFα production by pDCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: DENV-infected cells induced higher levels of IFNα and interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) as compared to synthetic TLR7/8 agonists (R848 and IMQ) in mouse pDCs.
source: DENV-infected cells induced higher levels of IFNα and interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) as compared to synthetic TLR7/8 agonists (R848 and IMQ) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D), results that were consistent with human pDC findings (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: The TLR7/8 agonist R848 induced a strong NF-κB-dependent gene signature in mouse pDCs, whereas limited induction was observed when using DENV-infected cells.
source: Conversely, the TLR7/8 agonist R848 induced a strong NF-κB-dependent gene signature in mouse pDCs, whereas limited induction was observed when using DENV-infected cells (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: pDC-mediated sensing of DENV-infected cells primarily leads to IFN-I production and a strong ISG response in the absence of NF-κB-mediated inflammatory responses.
source: Together, these results demonstrated that pDC-mediated sensing of DENV-infected cells primarily leads to IFN-I production and a strong ISG response in the absence of NF-κB-mediated inflammatory responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: A knock-in strain was established where Irf7 expression is driven by the pDC-specific Siglech promoter.
source: We established a knock-in strain where Irf7 expression is driven by the pDC-specific Siglech promoter (thus called SiglechIrf7/+) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the mouse model generation and Figure 2A.

claim: SiglechIrf7/+ mice were backcrossed onto Irf3-/-;Irf7-/- double knockout mice to generate hemizygous Irf7-expressing animals (SiglechIrf7/+;Irf3-/-;Irf7-/- referred to as 'pDC:Irf7+' mice).
source: We next backcrossed these mice onto Irf3-/-;Irf7-/- double knockout mice to generate hemizygous Irf7-expressing animals (SiglechIrf7/+;Irf3-/-;Irf7-/- referred to as 'pDC:Irf7+' mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the mouse model generation.

claim: Use of hemizygous mice preserved one copy of the Siglech gene.
source: Use of hemizygous mice preserved one copy of the Siglech gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the mouse model and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Irf3/7 double knockout mice are deficient in IFN-I production.
source: Irf3/7 double knockout mice (referred to as Irf3/7 DKO mice), deficient in IFN-I production (Rudd et al., 2012; Schilte et al., 2012) were used as comparator negative controls in all experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rudd et al., 2012 and Schilte et al., 2012.

claim: pDCs were the only cell type to retain significant levels of IRF7 protein expression in pDC:Irf7+ mice.
source: pDCs were the only cell type to retain significant levels of IRF7 protein expression, seen in both pDC:Irf7+ and WT mice, but not in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: IFN-I activity was observed in plasma/spleen of WT mice stimulated by TLR9 or TLR3 agonists, whereas little-to-no IFN-I activity was detected in Irf3/7 DKO mice.
source: As expected, we observed IFN-I activity in plasma/spleen of WT mice stimulated by either agonist, whereas little-to-no IFN-I activity was detected in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioassay data shown in Figure 2C–D.

claim: pDC:Irf7+ mice produced high levels of IFN-I in response to TLR9, but not TLR3 agonists.
source: Consistent with the TLR expression patterns in pDCs (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015), pDC:Irf7+ mice produced high levels of IFN-I in response to TLR9, but not TLR3 agonists.
evidence: This claim is supported by bioassay data and citation to Swiecki and Colonna, 2015.

claim: pDC:Irf7+ and WT pDCs produced similar amounts of IFNα when treated with TLR7 agonists or DENV-infected cells.
source: pDC:Irf7+ and WT pDCs produced similar amounts of IFNα (Figures 2E and 3A), confirming the functionality of IRF7 signaling in pDC:Irf7+ mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figures 2E and 3A.

claim: TNFα secretion levels in response to TLR7 agonists were comparable in pDCs from Irf3/7 DKO, pDC:Irf7+, and WT mice.
source: Confirming independent activation of NF-κB, we observed TNFα secretion levels in both strains to be comparable to WT mice (Figures 2F and 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figures 2F and 3B.

claim: ISGs previously defined as IRF5-dependent (e.g. Mx1, Ifit1) were still upregulated in Irf3/7 DKO pDCs when cocultured with DENV-infected cells or stimulated by other TLR7 agonists.
source: Of note, ISGs previously defined as IRF5-dependent (e.g. Mx1, Ifit1) (Lazear et al., 2013) were still upregulated in Irf3/7 DKO pDCs when cocultured with DENV-infected cells or stimulated by other TLR7 agonists (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and citation to Lazear et al., 2013.

claim: High levels of IFNα were detected in both the spleen and plasma of DENV-infected WT mice.
source: High levels of IFNα were detected in both the spleen and plasma of infected WT mice (Figure 3C–D), but not Irf3/7 DKO mice, in agreement with previous results (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3C–D and citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: IFNα was not detected in the spleen and plasma of DENV-infected Irf3/7 DKO mice.
source: High levels of IFNα were detected in both the spleen and plasma of infected WT mice (Figure 3C–D), but not Irf3/7 DKO mice, in agreement with previous results (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3C–D and citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: pDC:Irf7+ mice had undetectable IFNα/β levels in both the plasma and spleen at all analyzed times post-infection with DENV.
source: pDC:Irf7+ mice had undetectable IFNα/β levels in both the plasma and spleen at all analyzed times post-infection (p.i.) (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3C–D.

claim: Despite undetectable IFNα/β in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice, an early induction (i.e. 18 h p.i.) of ISG RNAs was observed in all tissues analyzed.
source: Importantly, despite undetectable IFNα/β in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice, an early induction (i.e. 18 h p.i.) of ISG RNAs was observed in all tissues analyzed.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data.

claim: Early induction of ISG RNAs was not observed in Irf3/7 DKO mice at 18 h p.i. with DENV.
source: By contrast, this early induction was not observed in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Basal ISG expression levels were lower in Irf3/7 DKO and pDC:Irf7+ mice compared to WT, likely reflecting diminished basal IFNAR signaling in the absence of Irf3 and Irf7.
source: Of note, basal ISG expression levels were lower in Irf3/7 DKO and pDC:Irf7+ mice compared to WT, likely reflecting diminished basal IFNAR signaling in the absence of Irf3 and Irf7 (Gough et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data and citation to Gough et al., 2012.

claim: Restricted expression of Irf7 in pDCs is sufficient to generate a systemic ISG response.
source: These results indicate that restricted expression of Irf7 in pDCs is sufficient to generate a systemic ISG response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: DENV infection induced ISGs and NF-κB-dependent transcripts in WT, but not Irf3/7 DKO mice.
source: DENV infection induced ISGs and NF-κB-dependent transcripts in WT, but not Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 3E–G; expressed as magnitude-independent Z score and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; expressed as magnitude-dependent fold-change), confirming previous findings (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 3E–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: Despite a strong upregulation of ISGs in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice, minimal induction of NF-κB-dependent inflammation-related transcripts was observed.
source: Strikingly, despite a strong upregulation of ISGs in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice, we observed minimal induction of NF-κB-dependent inflammation-related transcripts (Figure 3F–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 3F–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The principal signaling pathway downstream of DENV-activated pDCs is IRF7-dependent induction of the IFN-I pathway, which could be wholly segregated from the activation of NF-κB-induced cytokines.
source: Based on these in vivo and ex vivo observations, we concluded that the principal signaling pathway downstream of DENV-activated pDCs is IRF7-dependent induction of the IFN-I pathway, which could be wholly segregated from the activation of NF-κB-induced cytokines.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: At 42–72 hr post-infection, pDC:Irf7+ mice displayed significantly reduced levels of DENV titer and RNA in the spleen and plasma compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice.
source: Notably, at 42–72 hr post-infection, pDC:Irf7+ mice displayed significantly reduced levels of DENV titer and RNA in the spleen and plasma compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer and RNA quantification data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Viral titer and RNA levels were lower in WT mice than either Irf3/7 DKO or pDC:Irf7+ mice, likely due to the higher IFN-I response.
source: Viral titer and RNA levels were lower in WT mice than either Irf3/7 DKO or pDC:Irf7+ mice (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), likely due to the higher IFN-I response.
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer and RNA quantification data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The higher DENV levels in pDC:Irf7+ mice as compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice at early time points (i.e. 28 h p.i.) may reflect an enhanced recruitment of DENV-susceptible cells in the spleen of pDC:Irf7+ mice due to the localized pDC-induced IFN-I response.
source: The higher DENV levels in pDC:Irf7+ mice as compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice at early time points (i.e. 28 h p.i.) may reflect an enhanced recruitment of DENV-susceptible cells in the spleen of pDC:Irf7+ mice due to the localized pDC-induced IFN-I response (Schmid and Harris, 2014; Seo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to Schmid and Harris, 2014 and Seo et al., 2011.

claim: IRF7 expression in pDCs is sufficient to control DENV through the local production of IFN-I.
source: Our results indicate that IRF7 expression in pDCs is sufficient to control DENV through the local production of IFN-I.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Ifng and Gbp2 up-regulation temporally correlated with the induction of IFN-I-induced ISGs in DENV-infected Irf3/7 DKO mice.
source: Interestingly, Ifng and Gbp2 up-regulation (Figure 5B–C) temporally correlated with the induction of IFN-I-induced ISGs in DENV-infected Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 5A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 5A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E.

claim: ISGs including Ifit1/Usp18/Ifit3 respond more highly to IFN-I, but will still be induced to some extent by type II IFN.
source: Of note, these ISGs including Ifit1/Usp18/Ifit3 respond more highly to IFN-I, but will still be induced to some extent by type II IFN [(Chen et al., 2013; Hall et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012) and data not shown].
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013, Hall et al., 2012, and Liu et al., 2012.

claim: IFN-II signaling likely mediates the late induction of a larger set of ISGs observed in Irf3-/-/7-/- mice.
source: Therefore, in agreement with these prior studies, IFN-II signaling likely mediates the late induction of a larger set of ISGs observed in Irf3-/-/7-/- mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and prior studies.

claim: The kinetic profile of the type II IFN response was markedly different in pDC:Irf7+ mice as compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice, with Ifng and Gbp2 expression detected as early as 18 h p.i and peaking at 28 h p.i.
source: The kinetic profile of the type II IFN response was markedly different in pDC:Irf7 +mice as compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice, with Ifng and Gbp2 expression detected as early as 18 h p.i and peaking at 28 h p.i. (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR and ELISA data shown in Figures 5B–C.

claim: Early pDC IRF7-mediated signaling accelerates the IFN-II response, which is known to be part of the eventual control of DENV in mouse models.
source: This led to the compelling hypothesis that early pDC IRF7-mediated signaling accelerates the IFN-II response, which is known to be part of the eventual control of DENV in mouse models (Chen et al., 2013; Costa et al., 2017; Shresta et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013, Costa et al., 2017, and Shresta et al., 2004.

claim: IFNAR blockade in pDC:Irf7+ mice abrogated the early ISG response to DENV.
source: IFNAR blockade in pDC:Irf7+ mice abrogated this early ISG response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and correspondingly increased both DENV viremia in these mice, as readily observed in the spleen (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and to a lesser extent in the blood (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; not significant; likely as the consequence of the limited dynamic range of DENV detection at this time point in blood).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR and viral RNA quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, C, and D.

claim: IFNAR blockade in pDC:Irf7+ mice increased DENV viremia in the spleen.
source: IFNAR blockade in pDC:Irf7+ mice abrogated this early ISG response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and correspondingly increased both DENV viremia in these mice, as readily observed in the spleen (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and to a lesser extent in the blood (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; not significant; likely as the consequence of the limited dynamic range of DENV detection at this time point in blood).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral RNA quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ISG expression was still detected in the Irf3/7 DKO and pDC:Irf7+ at a later time point (72 h p.i.), suggesting that the late induction of ISGs is independent of pDC IRF7-mediated IFN-I and likely induced by IFN-II.
source: Of note, consistent with the results of Figure 5, ISG expression was still detected in the Irf3/7 DKO and pDC:Irf7+ at a later time point (72 h p.i.) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B), further suggesting that the late induction of ISGs is independent of pDC IRF7-mediated IFN-I and likely induced by IFN-II.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Recent work demonstrates that IRF1-mediated IFN-II can be induced by DENV, independent of Irf3/Irf7 expression.
source: Along the same line, recent work demonstrates that IRF1-mediated IFN-II can be induced by DENV, independent of Irf3/Irf7 expression (Carlin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Carlin et al., 2017.

claim: The IFNAR1-dependent response contributes to the control of DENV in Irf3/7 DKO mice.
source: In accordance, we showed that the IFNAR1-dependent response contributes to the control of DENV in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral RNA quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Despite undetectable IFN-I at a systemic level, the early ISG induction and control of DENV by the pDC-IRF7-induced response relies on IFN-I/IFNAR1 signaling.
source: Together, our results demonstrated that, despite undetectable IFN-I at a systemic level, the early ISG induction and control of DENV by the pDC-IRF7-induced response relies on IFN-I/IFNAR1 signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: An acceleration of IFN-II signaling was observed as a result of IRF7 expression in pDCs, temporally associated with viral control in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice.
source: Importantly, we also observed an acceleration of IFN-II signaling as a result of IRF7 expression in pDCs, temporally associated with viral control in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: An elevated fraction (~12%) of splenic NK cells produced IFNγ in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice.
source: We observed that an elevated fraction (~12%) of splenic NK cells produced IFNγ in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For other cell types, including NKT cells, γδ-T cells, αβ-T cells and neutrophils, IFNγ+ cells represented an extremely small fraction of total splenocytes.
source: For other cell types, including NKT cells, γδ-T cells, αβ-T cells and neutrophils, IFNγ+ cells represented an extremely small fraction of total splenocytes (Figure 6A, right panel and S5A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Splenic, but not blood-circulating NK cells, produced IFNγ protein in response to DENV infection.
source: Interestingly, splenic, but not blood-circulating NK cells, produced IFNγ protein in response to DENV infection, consistent with the absence of upregulation of blood Ifng mRNA (data not shown) and limited induction of the activation marker CD69 on blood NK cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NK cell response is localized to the spleen, the primary site of DENV replication.
source: This implies that NK cell response is localized to the spleen, the primary site of DENV replication.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The accelerated IFN-II response in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice was associated with an early recruitment of neutrophils to the spleen.
source: In agreement with a localized host response, we showed that the accelerated IFN-II response in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice was associated with an early recruitment of neutrophils to the spleen (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) as well as maturation of monocytes (identified as Ly6C++/Lineage- cells), as represented by upregulation of MHCII, which did not occur in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The accelerated IFN-II response in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice was associated with maturation of monocytes, as represented by upregulation of MHCII, which did not occur in Irf3/7 DKO mice.
source: In agreement with a localized host response, we showed that the accelerated IFN-II response in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice was associated with an early recruitment of neutrophils to the spleen (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) as well as maturation of monocytes (identified as Ly6C++/Lineage- cells), as represented by upregulation of MHCII, which did not occur in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both neutrophils and monocytes have been previously shown to be involved in the modulation of NK cell activation.
source: Of note, both cell types have been previously shown to be involved in the modulation of NK cell activation (Costa et al., 2017; Kang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Costa et al., 2017 and Kang et al., 2008.

claim: NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice lead to a significant increase of both splenic DENV RNA and viral titers.
source: An efficient depletion of NK cells (i.e. reduction by >80% of splenic and blood NK cells, Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) lead to a significant increase of both splenic DENV RNA and viral titers in pDC:Irf7+ mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer and RNA quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice was associated with a decrease in IFNγ mRNA, IFNγ protein and IFN-II ISG signature in the spleen and plasma.
source: This was associated with a decrease in IFNγ mRNA, IFNγ protein and IFN-II ISG signature in the spleen and plasma (Figure 6D–E), along with reduced neutrophil recruitment to the spleen and maturation of monocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA and qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 6D–E.

claim: NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice resulted in reduced neutrophil recruitment to the spleen and maturation of monocytes.
source: This was associated with a decrease in IFNγ mRNA, IFNγ protein and IFN-II ISG signature in the spleen and plasma (Figure 6D–E), along with reduced neutrophil recruitment to the spleen and maturation of monocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–C.

claim: IFN-I-induced ISG levels were not impacted by NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice at 48 h p.i.
source: Closing the circle and establishing IFNα responses as upstream, we observed that IFN-I-induced ISG levels were not impacted by NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice at 48 h p.i. (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Human pDCs produced robust IFNα in response to CHIKV only when in contact with CHIKV-infected cells.
source: We tested whether pDC activation by CHIKV shares the same features as DENV, showing that indeed, human pDCs produced robust IFNα in response to CHIKV only when in contact with CHIKV-infected cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Robust IFNα levels were detected when WT mouse pDCs were co-cultured with CHIKV infected Vero cells or with syngeneic co-cultures of Irf3/7 DKO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs).
source: Similarly, robust IFNα levels were detected when WT mouse pDCs were co-cultured with CHIKV infected Vero cells or with syngeneic co-cultures of Irf3/7 DKO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by SiMoA assay data shown in Figures 7B–C.

claim: Cell-free CHIKV and CHIKV-infected cells physically separated from pDCs did not induce IFNα secretion.
source: By contrast, cell-free CHIKV and CHIKV-infected cells physically separated from pDCs did not induce IFNα secretion (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA and SiMoA assay data shown in Figures 7A–B.

claim: CHIKV-infected cells failed to activate pDCs deficient for Tlr7.
source: CHIKV-infected cells failed to activate pDCs deficient for Tlr7, whereas pDCs deficient for Mavs (i.e. the downstream signaling adaptor of RLR pathway) produced levels of IFNα comparable to WT pDCs (Figure 7D and data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by SiMoA assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: pDCs deficient for Mavs produced levels of IFNα comparable to WT pDCs in response to CHIKV-infected cells.
source: CHIKV-infected cells failed to activate pDCs deficient for Tlr7, whereas pDCs deficient for Mavs (i.e. the downstream signaling adaptor of RLR pathway) produced levels of IFNα comparable to WT pDCs (Figure 7D and data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by SiMoA assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The sensing of CHIKV-infected cells by pDCs led to an IRF7-mediated cytokine production (IFNα), but not NF-κB-induced inflammatory cytokines (TNFα).
source: Comparable to DENV-induced responses, the sensing of CHIKV-infected cells by pDCs led to an IRF7-mediated cytokine production (IFNα), but not NF-κB-induced inflammatory cytokines (TNFα) (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: pDC induction by CHIKV required the cell-to-cell sensing of infected cells by TLR7-induced signaling and led to an IRF7-restricted response.
source: Together, this demonstrated that, like DENV, pDC induction by CHIKV required the cell-to-cell sensing of infected cells by TLR7-induced signaling and led to an IRF7-restricted response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: WT mice showed no clinical symptoms to CHIKV infection, whereas Irf3/7 DKO mice rapidly succumbed to CHIKV infection.
source: Mice were infected s.c. with CHIKV, and as previously reported WT mice showed no clinical symptoms, whereas Irf3/7 DKO mice rapidly succumbed to CHIKV infection (Figure 7F) (Schilte et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7F and citation to Schilte et al., 2012.

claim: pDC:Irf7+ mice experienced no overt clinical symptoms with 100% of mice surviving CHIKV infection.
source: By contrast, pDC:Irf7+ mice experienced no overt clinical symptoms with 100% of mice surviving infection (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Early control of CHIKV viremia was improved in pDC:Irf7+ mice compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice, although reduced as compared to WT mice.
source: Early control of viremia was improved in pDC:Irf7+ mice compared to Irf3/7 DKO mice, although reduced as compared to WT mice (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: By day 7 p.i., pDC:Irf7+ mice had cleared CHIKV infections.
source: By day 7 p.i., pDC:Irf7+ mice had cleared CHIKV infections (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated but data is not shown.

claim: There was differential control of CHIKV in pDC:Irf7+ mice depending on the tissue.
source: Importantly, there was differential control of CHIKV in pDC:Irf7+ mice depending on the tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The initial sites of CHIKV replication (i.e. the infection site: skin/muscle and muscle) displayed relatively higher viral titers as compared to more distal sites (i.e. the spleen and liver), where virus was barely detectable at 48 h p.i. in pDC:Irf7+ mice.
source: The initial sites of CHIKV replication (i.e. the infection site: skin/muscle and muscle) displayed relatively higher viral titers as compared to more distal sites (i.e. the spleen and liver), where virus was barely detectable at 48 h p.i. in pDC:Irf7+ mice (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The pDC antiviral response may control infection once virus spreads systematically, as previously proposed in the context of Herpes Simplex virus infection.
source: It is possible that the pDC antiviral response controls infection once virus spreads systematically, as previously proposed in the context of Herpes Simplex virus infection (Swiecki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to Swiecki et al., 2013.

claim: Plasma IFNα remained undetectable in CHIKV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice at both 24 and 48 h p.i. using a highly sensitive Single Molecule Assay (SiMoA).
source: We established a mouse IFNα Single Molecule Assay (SiMoA) (Rissin et al., 2010), with a quantification limit at 0.1 pg/ml (i.e. >100 fold increased sensitivity compared to current assays, data not shown). Nonetheless plasma IFNα remained undetectable in CHIKV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice at both 24 and 48 h p.i. (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated but data is not shown, and is supported by citation to Rissin et al., 2010.

claim: IFNAR blockade in pDC:Irf7+ mice induced lethality and greatly increased CHIKV viremia.
source: Therefore, we validated the dependence on IFN-I-induced signaling for the control of CHIK by pDCs using IFNAR1 blocking antibody. IFNAR blockade in pDC:Irf7+ mice induced lethality and, consistently, greatly increased CHIKV viremia (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival and viral titer data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: IFNAR1-dependent response did not contribute to the control of CHIKV in Irf3/7 DKO mice.
source: By contrast with results for DENV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), IFNAR1-dependent response did contribute to the control of CHIKV in Irf3/7 DKO mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The discrepancy between DENV and CHIKV infections in IFNAR1 contribution likely reflects the greater impact of IFN-I signaling in CHIKV versus DENV infection and/or a differential contribution of the alternate IRF-mediated signal transduction.
source: This discrepancy between DENV and CHIKV infections likely reflects the greater impact of IFN-I signaling in CHIKV versus DENV infection and/or a differential contribution of the alternate IRF-mediated signal transduction.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the experimental observations.

claim: NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice increased CHIKV titers (~10 fold-increase, although not statistically significant).
source: Similar to DENV, NK cell depletion in pDC:Irf7+ mice increased CHIKV titers (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, ~10 fold-increase, although not statistically significant).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IRF7 expression in pDCs is sufficient to control two genetically distant RNA viruses (CHIKV and DENV) via the local production of IFN-I and IFNγ secretion by NK cells.
source: Together, these data indicate that IRF7 expression in pDCs is sufficient to control two genetically distant RNA viruses (CHIKV and DENV) via the local production of IFN-I and IFNγ secretion by NK cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: pDCs are a key cell type in the initiation of antiviral responses to DENV and CHIKV.
source: We provide compelling evidence that pDCs are a key cell type in the initiation of antiviral responses to these two distinct RNA viruses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: pDC activation by DENV/CHIKV is characterized by IRF7-prioritized signaling, while passively excluding NF-κB-mediated responses.
source: We demonstrate that pDC activation by DENV/CHIKV is characterized by IRF7-prioritized signaling, while passively excluding NF-κB-mediated responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Despite undetectable levels of systemic IFN-I, pDC IRF7 signaling is critical for the induction of a potent antiviral response.
source: Despite undetectable levels of systemic IFN-I, pDC IRF7 signaling is critical for the induction of a potent antiviral response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: pDC IRF7 signaling might reflect a local pDC IFN-I response and is in keeping with the requirement for physical contact with infected cells to activate pDCs.
source: This might reflect a local pDC IFN-I response and is in keeping with the requirement for physical contact with infected cells to activate pDCs, in turn inducing a potent ISG response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: pDC-IRF7 activation accelerates NK-mediated IFN-II induction, which assists in control of viremia.
source: Notably, pDC-IRF7 activation accelerates NK-mediated IFN-II induction, which assists in control of viremia.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: pDCs have previously been demonstrated to be required for the control of several viral infections, including herpes simplex virus (HSV), murine hepatitis virus (MHV), murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV), vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV).
source: pDCs have previously been demonstrated to be required for the control of several viral infections, including herpes simplex virus (HSV), murine hepatitis virus (MHV), murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV), vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Swiecki and Colonna, 2015.

claim: Others reported that pDCs are dispensable and/or do not contribute to IFN-I production in the case of certain infections, including influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), Newcastle disease virus (NDV) and MCMV.
source: In contrast, others reported that pDCs are dispensable and/or do not contribute to IFN-I production in the case of certain infections, including influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), Newcastle disease virus (NDV) and MCMV (Del Prete et al., 2015; GeurtsvanKessel et al., 2008; Jewell et al., 2007; Kumagai et al., 2007; Swiecki et al., 2013), which may be a reflection of viral replication mechanisms, inoculum size, or location (Swiecki et al., 2010; Swiecki et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Del Prete et al., 2015, GeurtsvanKessel et al., 2008, Jewell et al., 2007, Kumagai et al., 2007, Swiecki et al., 2013, Swiecki et al., 2010.

claim: While antiviral response (i.e. IFN-I production) in infected cells acts as a first line defense, pDCs may serve as a failsafe, triggered upon systemic infection and therefore failure of viral control.
source: These observations bring the emerging concept that while antiviral response (i.e. IFN-I production) in infected cells acts as a first line defense, pDCs may serve as a failsafe, triggered upon systemic infection and therefore failure of viral control (GarciaGarcía-Sastre, 2017; Tomasello et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to García-Sastre, 2017 and Tomasello et al., 2014.

claim: This assumption is in line with the multiple inhibitory mechanisms of antiviral sensing by viral proteins expressed by infected cells.
source: This assumption is in line with the multiple inhibitory mechanisms of antiviral sensing by viral proteins expressed by infected cells (GarciaGarcía-Sastre, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to García-Sastre, 2017.

claim: Previous investigations have primarily demonstrated the importance of pDCs in viral control by depletion of pDCs.
source: Nonetheless, previous investigations have primarily demonstrated the importance of pDCs in viral control by depletion of pDCs (Swiecki and Colonna, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Swiecki and Colonna, 2015.

claim: The pDC:Irf7+ model offers a unique opportunity to define pDC function.
source: Here, we validated a model consisting of a pDC-restricted IFN response, which offers a unique opportunity to define pDC function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the development and validation of the mouse model.

claim: The pDC:Irf7+ model permitted the study of the possible cryptic pDC-mediated control of certain infections.
source: This new model also permitted the study of the possible cryptic pDC-mediated control of certain infections.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the development and validation of the mouse model.

claim: pDC antiviral function might be masked due to the homeostasis of the innate immunity, including an enhanced response by other cell types when pDCs are depleted.
source: For instance, pDC antiviral function might be masked due to the homeostasis of the innate immunity, including an enhanced response by other cell types when pDCs are depleted.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation.

claim: pDCs are sufficient to initiate early control of viral infections, via induction of IRF7-prone signaling.
source: We demonstrated that pDCs are sufficient to initiate early control of viral infections, via induction of IRF7-prone signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Irf7 overexpression artifacts are avoided in the pDC:IRF7+ model as Irf7 steady-state expression is reduced under the control of the Siglech promoter relative to the Irf7 promoter.
source: However, Irf7 overexpression artifacts are avoided in the pDC:IRF7+ model as Irf7 steady-state expression is reduced under the control of the Siglech promoter relative to the Irf7 promoter (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Siglech expression by pDCs is inversely correlated to ISG upregulation in vivo.
source: Furthermore, Siglech expression by pDCs is inversely correlated to ISG upregulation in vivo (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), in agreement with prior study (Puttur et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and citation to Puttur et al., 2013.

claim: pDCs respond in a contact-dependent manner to infected cells, and thus induce highly localized IFN-dependent responses.
source: Therefore, in line with our ex vivo results in this and previous studies (Décembre et al., 2014), we propose that pDCs respond in a contact-dependent manner to infected cells, and thus induce highly localized IFN-dependent responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented and citation to Décembre et al., 2014.

claim: The localized pDC IFN response is sufficient to impart a large-scale antiviral response, which protects from viral infections.
source: Importantly, this response is sufficient to impart a large-scale antiviral response, which protects from viral infections.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The engagement of TLR7/9 leading to IFN-I production and NF-κB-dependent pro-inflammatory cytokines by pDCs may affect downstream immunological parameters, such as B cell differentiation induced by pDC response to influenza virus.
source: The engagement of TLR7/9 leading to IFN-I production and NF-κB-dependent pro-inflammatory cytokines by pDCs may affect downstream immunological parameters, such as for example, B cell differentiation induced by pDC response to influenza virus (Jego et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jego et al., 2003.

claim: pDCs fail to respond via NF-κB-mediated inflammatory responses to DENV/CHIKV-infected cells, indicating that pDC TLR7 signaling induced by these viruses primarily leads to IRF7 induction.
source: We observed that pDCs fail to respond via NF-κB-mediated inflammatory responses to DENV/CHIKV-infected cells, indicating that pDC TLR7 signaling induced by these viruses primarily leads to IRF7 induction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: On the whole-organism level, while ectopic IRF7 expression in pDCs fully restores ISG responses, NF-κB responses to DENV were absent in both pDC:Irf7+ and Irf3/7 DKO mice.
source: Consistently, on the whole-organism level, while ectopic IRF7 expression in pDCs fully restores ISG responses, NF-κB responses to DENV were absent in both pDC:Irf7+ and Irf3/7 DKO mice, thus underlining the importance of the IRF7 and dispensability of the NF-κB responses in pDC-mediated control of DENV and CHIKV infections.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: NF-κB induction by DENV and CHIKV in other cell types likely requires cross-talk between IRF3 and NF-κB.
source: Our results also imply that NF-κB induction by these viruses in other cell types likely requires cross-talk between IRF3 and NF-κB (Freaney et al., 2013; Iwanaszko and Kimmel, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Freaney et al., 2013 and Iwanaszko and Kimmel, 2015.

claim: pDC IFN-I responses were important in early control of both DENV and CHIKV infections in vivo, but substantial differences were observed in the overall outcome of infections.
source: While pDC IFN-I responses were important in early control of both DENV and CHIKV infections in vivo, substantial differences were observed in the overall outcome of infections.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: CHIKV infections were invariably lethal in the Irf3/7 DKO genetic background, and pDC IFN-I responses provided 100% protection to this lethal phenotype.
source: CHIKV infections were invariably lethal in the Irf3/7 DKO genetic background, and pDC IFN-I responses provided 100% protection to this lethal phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: DENV infections were well-controlled even in Irf3/7 DKO mice by 72 h p.i.
source: By contrast, DENV infections were well-controlled even in Irf3/7 DKO mice by 72 h p.i.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: pDC IFN-I responses lead to substantial control of DENV viremia at time points intermediate between WT and Irf3/7 DKO mice (~42–48 hr).
source: Notably, pDC IFN-I responses lead to substantial control of DENV viremia at time points intermediate between WT and Irf3/7 DKO mice (~42–48 hr).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The lethal phenotype in CHIKV infection in Irf3/7 DKO mice correlated with substantially higher viral titers, as compared to DENV levels.
source: In our study, the lethal phenotype in CHIKV infection in Irf3/7 DKO mice correlated with substantially higher viral titers, as compared to DENV levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Blockade of IFN-I signaling in Irf3/7 DKO mice only increased viremia in situations where lower basal viral titers were observed.
source: Interestingly, blockade of IFN-I signaling in Irf3/7 DKO mice only increased viremia in situations where lower basal viral titers were observed: for example, DENV infections in all organs, or CHIKV viral titers in the liver.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The persistence of IFN-I-mediated viral control under conditions of lower basal viral titers depends on IRF5 or IRF1 signaling.
source: We thus suggest that the persistence of IFN-I-mediated viral control under these conditions depends on IRF5 or IRF1 signaling (Carlin et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2013; Lazear et al., 2013; Rudd et al., 2012), as control of flaviviral infections is still contingent on IFNAR signaling in the absence of Irf3/Irf7 expression.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to Carlin et al., 2017, Chen et al., 2013, Lazear et al., 2013, and Rudd et al., 2012.

claim: The contribution of alternate IRF proteins to the antiviral response may only be revealed in case of relatively low viremia.
source: The contribution of these alternate IRF proteins to the antiviral response may only be revealed in case of relatively low viremia.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the experimental observations.

claim: Eventual control of DENV in the Irf3/7 DKO background depended on the induced IFNγ response.
source: Eventual control of DENV in the Irf3/7 DKO background depended on the induced IFNγ response (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: An IFN-II response is observed in DENV-infected Irf3/7 DKO mice peaking at ~42 h p.i., which is largely absent in WT mice.
source: In agreement, we observe an IFN-II response in DENV-infected Irf3/7 DKO mice peaking at ~42 h p.i., which is largely absent in WT mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The pDC-regulated IFN-II responses are consistent with prior work showing a defect in type II IFN activation in a pDC-deficient mouse model.
source: These pDC-regulated IFN-II responses are consistent with prior work showing a defect in type II IFN activation in a pDC-deficient mouse model (Guillerey et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guillerey et al., 2012.

claim: IFNγ production in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice is largely mediated by NK cells in the spleen, the primary site of DENV replication.
source: We demonstrated that IFNγ production in DENV-infected pDC:Irf7+ mice is largely mediated by NK cells in the spleen, the primary site of DENV replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Activated NK cells mediate downstream IFN-II responses that contribute to control of DENV viremia, in accordance with a recent report.
source: These activated NK cells mediate downstream IFN-II responses that contribute to control of DENV viremia, in accordance with a recent report (Costa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and citation to Costa et al., 2017.

claim: DENV may be more sensitive to type II IFN signaling (relative to type I IFN) compared to CHIKV, as DENV infections cause higher lethality in Ifngr-/- compared to Ifnar-/- mice, a situation that is reversed in the context of CHIKV infection.
source: DENV may be more sensitive to type II IFN signaling (relative to type I IFN) compared to CHIKV, as DENV infections cause higher lethality in Ifngr-/- compared to Ifnar-/- mice, a situation that is reversed in the context of CHIKV infection (Gardner et al., 2012; Shresta et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gardner et al., 2012 and Shresta et al., 2004.

claim: IFNγ production by NK cells was not observed in the blood, a site of low DENV viremia, likely indicating a necessity for NK cells to be closely apposed to DENV-infected cells and/or DENV-activated cells to achieve NK cell activation of IFN-II responses.
source: Importantly, IFNγ production by NK cells was not observed in the blood, a site of low DENV viremia, likely indicating a necessity for NK cells to be closely apposed to DENV-infected cells and/or DENV-activated cells to achieve NK cell activation of IFN-II responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: A pDC IRF7-mediated influx of neutrophils and monocyte activation was observed in the spleens of DENV-infected mice.
source: We also observed an association with other immune cell parameters, including a pDC IRF7-mediated influx of neutrophils and monocyte activation in the spleens of DENV-infected mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Some reports suggested that type I IFN directly contributes to NK cell response.
source: While some reports suggested that type I IFN directly contributes to NK cell response, NF-κB-dependent cytokines are well-known to regulate IFNγ production by NK cells (Schulthess et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schulthess et al., 2012.

claim: NF-κB-dependent cytokines are well-known to regulate IFNγ production by NK cells.
source: While some reports suggested that type I IFN directly contributes to NK cell response, NF-κB-dependent cytokines are well-known to regulate IFNγ production by NK cells (Schulthess et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schulthess et al., 2012.

claim: In vitro studies suggested that pDCs act in concert with monocytes to potentiate NK-cell-mediated IFNγ production in the context of HCV and DENV infection.
source: Along the same lines, in vitro studies suggested that pDCs act in concert with monocytes to potentiate NK-cell-mediated IFNγ production in the context of HCV and DENV infection (Costa et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Costa et al., 2017 and Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: The ability to segregate NF-κB and IRF7 responses may have potential use in developing novel therapies.
source: The ability to segregate NF-κB and IRF7 responses may have potential use in developing novel therapies.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: NF-κB-dependent cytokines have been associated with disease severity in both DENV and CHIKV infection.
source: Notably, NF-κB-dependent cytokines have been associated with disease severity in both DENV and CHIKV infection (Chen et al., 2007; Dupuis-Maguiraga et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2007 and Dupuis-Maguiraga et al., 2012.

claim: pDC-derived IFN responses support viral clearance while avoiding possible inflammatory responses.

claim: This study provides an important indication of how early viral control may be mediated by one of the key drivers of the IFN response, the plasmacytoid dendritic cell.
source: As arboviral infections tend to be acute, rather than chronic diseases, this study provides an important indication of how early viral control may be mediated by one of the key drivers of the IFN response, the plasmacytoid dendritic cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.
